title: Multisyllabic Words: How I Help Students Unlock Statistical Learning
author: Catlin Goodrow
summary: A reading interventionist takes up Mark Seidenberg's provocative claim that the science of reading wrongly assumes everything must be explicitly taught, and shows how she uses statistical (implicit) learning with older intervention students. She argues this is not balanced literacy: students first need solid foundational skills and a flexible sense that letter combinations map to a range of plausible pronunciations. She scaffolds multisyllabic word reading by dividing words, then teaches a simple, flexible strategy that students soon generalize. The readiness signal is students correctly reading words with patterns never explicitly taught, which tells her it is time to move toward structured knowledge-building units. Her conclusion is that implicit learning supplements, rather than replaces, explicit and systematic instruction.
points: Seidenberg's point is that brains are statistical pattern finders, so not every grapheme-phoneme combination needs explicit teaching.
This differs from balanced literacy because it rests on foundational phonics knowledge plus flexibility (set for variability), not cueing.
Older intervention students are scaffolded by dividing multisyllabic words, then taught a simple strategy they quickly generalize and abbreviate.
Readiness for less explicit teaching shows when students read words with patterns never explicitly taught, which requires giving them non-decodable text.
Explicit, systematic principles stay in place; they are applied differently once students are self-teaching.
quotes: Seidenberg was referring to the fact that our brains are statistical pattern finders; as kids read, their brains are picking up patterns that are not explicitly taught. This is referred to as implicit learning, statistical learning, or self-teaching.

In order to do so, students need to have a good grounding in foundational skills, but also know to be flexible, particularly with vowel sounds and consonant digraphs that have multiple pronunciations (also known as "set for variability").
I find many older intervention students don't have strategies in place for reading words of 2+ syllables. I begin to scaffold by dividing the words for students

I notice that my students are reading more and more words that contain patterns that we haven't learned explicitly. (You have to give kids chances to read non-decodable text to find this out!) When this happens, I have a good idea that they are ready to move away from highly-explicit phonics teaching, and into structured, knowledge-building units.

So, yes, we need to set students up for implicit/statistical learning as they read. We can not teach every phonics pattern that kids will encounter, and so we need to give them opportunities to read less-controlled text.
But that doesn't mean we let go of the principles of explicit, systematic instruction. We just do it in a different way.
